the-forest-of-love-2019.gazette: Between 1996 and 1998, in a Fukuoka apartment, a man used electric shocks, manufactured debt, and enforced isolation to make a family kill its own members; the case broke only when a teenage relative escaped and walked into a police station. Japanese coverage stayed muted, and the trial record remains the fullest public account of what happened in those rooms. Sono keeps the mechanism — the household turned into an instrument — and changes the names.

the-conjuring-the-devil-made-me-do-it-20.gazette: In 1981 a Connecticut defense team asked a court to accept demonic possession as grounds for a killing in Brookfield. The judge ruled it inadmissible, the jury returned first-degree manslaughter, and the defendant served roughly five years. The transcript is a public document, which is more than most horror pictures leave behind.

navalny-2022.gazette: Bellingcat assembled the poisoning case out of telecom and travel records bought on Russia's grey data market, matching a security team's movements to Navalny's. Then Navalny placed the call himself, and an FSB chemist described where the nerve agent had been applied before working out who was asking. The camera was in the room for it.
navalny-2022.prism: That method only worked once — an open data market, a bureaucrat who picked up the phone. Both have since closed, and the man who made the call died in a penal colony above the Arctic Circle.

20-days-in-mariupol-2023.gazette: AP's three-person team, led by Mstyslav Chernov, were the last international journalists inside Mariupol, filing until the city's connections went dark in March 2022. The maternity hospital footage left on hard drives carried out through Russian checkpoints in a police convoy. It circulated as evidence before it was ever cut into a film.

killers-of-the-flower-moon-2023.gazette: Oil under Osage land made headright holders among the wealthiest people per capita in the United States in the 1920s, and Oklahoma courts answered by assigning white guardians to manage their money. Dozens of Osage died in the years that followed; the federal investigation reached only a portion of them. The production worked with Osage consultants on language, dress, and ceremony, and descendants are still counting the dead the Bureau never got to.

origin-2023.gazette: Wilkerson researched Caste across three continents — the 1933 book burnings in Berlin, Jim Crow ordinance, Dalit life in India — and lost her husband and her mother in the years the work took. DuVernay filmed the research itself, archives and deaths included. Studios passed on it; philanthropic funders paid for it instead.
origin-2023.prism: Making an argument watchable meant putting the scholar's grief on screen next to her footnotes, a trade most nonfiction never has to make. And the picture nobody would finance is the one claiming that hierarchies outlast everyone who builds them.

the-eternal-memory-2023.gazette: Góngora spent the dictatorship filming what Chilean television would not broadcast, work that moved through the country on smuggled cassettes under the name Teleanálisis. Decades on, Alzheimer's took the memory of a man who had spent a career keeping the nation's. He died in 2023; the archive he built did not go with him.

black-box-diaries-2024.gazette: Ito's case rested on hotel security footage and a taxi driver's account, after a criminal arrest warrant was cancelled without public explanation. She won damages in a 2019 civil judgment and kept recording throughout. The film has screened across the world and has yet to open in Japan.

sugarcane-2024.gazette: After Kamloops announced suspected unmarked graves in 2021, Williams Lake First Nation opened its own investigation into St. Joseph's Mission, which took local children until 1981. The inquiry documented infants born to students at the school and what was done with them. One of the filmmakers' fathers was among those newborns.
sugarcane-2024.prism: The investigator and the evidence are the same family here, which is what happens when an institution runs long enough to reach the people now obliged to count its dead. The record wasn't lost — it was held, and it took a Nation's own commission to get at it.

the-girl-with-the-needle-2024.gazette: Copenhagen's 1921 trial of Dagmar Overbye ended in a death sentence, later commuted, for killing infants handed to her by women with no lawful way to give them up. She was convicted on a fraction of the deaths investigators believed she caused. Denmark rewrote its adoption and child-welfare law in the aftermath.

come-and-see-1985.gazette: Adamovich gathered the testimony himself, going village to village in Belarus for the book that became the screenplay; 628 Belarusian villages were burned with their inhabitants inside during the occupation. Klimov shot at Khatyn, where one of them had stood, after the script sat with Soviet censors for years. Live rounds were fired over the actors during production.

shoah-1985.gazette: Lanzmann worked eleven years and shot some 350 hours of film, and used not a single frame of archive. Every image is a face in the present tense — survivors, Polish villagers living beside the rail lines, former SS men recorded on a hidden camera. The sites were filmed as they stood: fields, sidings, forest.
shoah-1985.prism: Refusing the archive was an argument, not a style — that the footage the perpetrators shot is their version, and testimony has to be taken face to face. It cost eleven years, and it means the film can never be made again. The witnesses are gone.

the-official-story-1985.gazette: Puenzo shot in Buenos Aires while the junta's own generals were going on trial, barely a year after the dictatorship ended. The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo estimate some 500 infants were taken from disappeared prisoners and placed with other families. More than a hundred have been identified since, and the search has never closed.

grave-of-the-fireflies-1988.gazette: Nosaka was fourteen when incendiary bombs burned Kobe in 1945; his household was destroyed in the raid and his younger sister died of malnutrition in the months after. He wrote the story two decades later and described it as an apology to her. Takahata's adaptation opened in Japanese theatres on a double bill with My Neighbor Totoro.

black-rain-1989.gazette: Ibuse assembled his 1965 novel from hibakusha diaries and interviews, keeping the flat register of the original entries. Imamura filmed it in black and white twenty-four years later, staying with the years after the blast rather than the blast — the marriage that falls through, the sickness that arrives late. Hiroshima survivors were still being refused work and matches when the book was written.
black-rain-1989.prism: The bomb takes about a minute of screen time; the shunning takes decades. That's what the diaries actually recorded, and it needed a novelist and then a filmmaker before anyone would sit with it.
